en: Chlorophyll in leaves absorbs sunlight to convert water and carbon dioxide into glucose for plant energy.
The Arctic fox grows thick white winter fur to camouflage in snow and trap body heat.
Stomach acid breaks down chewed food into a liquid mixture so intestines can absorb its nutrients.
When wolves hunt sick elk, they prevent overgrazing by keeping the elk population from growing too large.
Bees transfer pollen between flower parts while collecting nectar, which fertilizes the plant to produce seeds.
The heart pumps oxygen-rich blood through arteries to deliver oxygen to cells throughout the entire body.
A caterpillar digests its own body inside a chrysalis to reorganize its cells into a butterfly.
White blood cells produce antibodies that attach to specific invading germs to destroy them and prevent illness.
Transpiration from leaves pulls water and dissolved minerals up through the xylem tubes from the plant roots.
Fish push water over their gills, where thin blood vessels absorb dissolved oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
Sensory nerves send electrical signals from the skin to the brain, which processes the feeling of touch.
Fungi secrete enzymes that break down dead leaves into simple nutrients, returning them to the soil for plants.
